title: Epsilon Removal from a Thompson NFA
description: Computes the ε-closure for each state, builds an equivalent ε-free NFA by the formula closure(move(closure({q}), x)), and verifies both NFAs accept the same strings up to length 6.
source: draft: opencode free model + edit: codex

steps.description: The Thompson NFA for `(a|b)*abb` with states 0 through 10. `EPS` maps each state to its ε-targets (e.g., 0 goes to 1 and 7). `MOVE` maps `(state, symbol)` pairs to target states for `a` and `b`. `START=0`, `ACCEPT={10}`.

`closure(S)` computes every state reachable from `S` by ε-moves alone, including `S` itself. It uses a stack for depth-first search: pop a state, follow its ε-arrows, add unseen targets to `out` and push them. `EPS.get(q, ())` returns an empty tuple when a state has no ε-moves.
`move(S, x)` returns every state reachable from `S` by exactly one symbol `x`. The set comprehension iterates each `q` in `S` and collects `MOVE.get((q, x), ())`. Missing transitions yield empty.

steps.question: The comment on line 26 says the new delta is `closure(move(closure({q}), x))`. Why are there two calls to `closure`?
steps.answer: The inner `closure({q})` expands `q` to all states reachable by ε-moves before reading the symbol. `move` takes one `x`-step from that set. The outer `closure` then expands the result by any ε-moves that follow the `x`-step. Both before and after the symbol, ε-moves can fire.

steps.description: The loop builds the ε-free NFA. For each state `q`, it computes `cq = closure({q})`. For each symbol `a` and `b`, it sets `new_delta[(q, x)] = closure(move(cq, x))`. If `cq` intersects `ACCEPT`, state `q` becomes accepting in the new NFA. The print shows each state's closure and its new `a` and `b` transitions.

Two runner functions verify equivalence. `run_eps_nfa` simulates the original: starts at `closure({START})`, then for each character does `closure(move(cur, ch))`. `run_new_nfa` simulates the ε-free version: starts at `{START}` and uses `new_delta` directly.
Run it. The `try` block starts and the loop over `STATES` begins.
For state 0, `closure({0})` computes `[0, 1, 2, 4, 7]` (following ε from 0 to 1,7; from 1 to 2,4; from 7 to nothing new). The print shows this closure and the new `a` and `b` transitions.
The loop continues for states 1 through 10, printing each row. The output shows closures growing as ε-paths chain together.
The accepting states in the new NFA print: `accepting: [0, 1, 3, 5, 6, 7]`  -  any state whose closure contains 10 becomes accepting.
The test generates all strings over `{a, b}` up to length 6. Both runners are called on each, and `agree` is `True`  -  the ε-free NFA accepts exactly the same language.
